newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav businessmen urge return to world community.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav businessmen urge return to world community.

text.p: Yugoslav businessmen said on Monday the government needed to do more to restore ties to the international community if it wanted to reach proposed 1997 economic targets.
"It is unlikely that our economy in the state it is in will reach the projected economic growth," Momcilo Zivkovic of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce said.
"Yugoslavia must restore its ties with the international community if it wants to achieve any significant growth," he told Reuters.

Zivkovic, who chairs the chamber's board for economic cooperation with the world, said managers expected the state to provide a favourable economic climate and create conditions for normal and regular business.
"We demand from the government to speed up its activities regarding the country's full reintegration into international financial institutions," he said.
The government proposal for 1997 economic policy sees up to 13 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP).
It projected an increase of up to 48 percent in exports, a rise in industrial production up to 13.9 percent and up to 6 percent expansion of agricultural production.
Svetozar Krasin, secretary to the chamber's board, said a lack of working capital which burdened the Yugoslav economy could not be resolved without financial help from abroad.

"Restoring ties with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank are top priorities for revival of our cash-starved economy," he said. "Without it we cannot make one single step forward."

The crippling U.N. trade and oil sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, for its role in the Bosnian war have isolated the country from the international community and blocked access to foreign funds.
The sanctions were lifted last October, but the so called "outer wall" of sanctions remains in place, preventing Belgrade from obtaining badly needed capital.
Businessmen said contradictory federal and republican laws were also discouraging investment.
"Frequent changes of laws and regulations have put off many foreign investors," said Milan Njegomir, director of the Yugoslav livestock fund.
But political analysts warned a political crisis sparked by alleged fraud during local elections could slow down attempts to rejoin the international community.

"Respect of basic human rights is one of the main prerequisites for Belgrade's equal treatment in the international community," said one analyst. "This will damage Yugoslavia's image in the world and postpone its readmittance in the IMF and the World Bank." -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
